parts.title: UPSC Economy: Taxation in India
parts.intro: Today we study the 'Revenue Stream'. Taxes are the primary source of government income. We explore the shift from a complex tax regime to the 'Goods and Services Tax' (GST) and the importance of 'Direct' vs 'Indirect' taxes. For UPSC, focus on 'Laffer Curve', 'Tax-to-GDP ratio', and the concept of 'Tax Buoyancy'. Let's master the logic of taxation today.

pages.title: Direct Taxes
pages.intro: Taxes where the payer and the bearer of the burden are the same person, progressive in nature.

items.label: Incidence vs Impact
items.value: Same entity; burden cannot be shifted

items.label: Nature
items.value: Progressive – higher income, higher tax rate

items.label: Contrast
items.value: Unlike indirect taxes (e.g., GST) where payer ≠ bearer

pages.title: Indirect Taxes
pages.intro: Taxes added to the price of goods/services, where the payer collects from the consumer and remits to the government.

blocks.text: Indirect taxes are charges added to the price of goods and services. The person paying the tax to the government (e.g., a shopkeeper) is different from the person who bears the economic burden (the consumer). Examples include GST, excise duty, and customs duty. These taxes are regressive in nature, as they take a larger percentage of income from lower-income groups.

pages.title: GST (Goods and Services Tax)
pages.intro: A single, destination-based indirect tax under 'One Nation, One Tax', with a dual structure. Since 22 September 2025 it has two main rates, 5% and 18%, plus 40% for luxury and sin goods.

pages.title: Laffer Curve
pages.intro: Illustrates that beyond a revenue-maximizing rate, higher tax rates reduce total tax revenue due to disincentives and evasion.

blocks.text: Common mistake: Assuming higher tax rates always increase revenue. Beyond the optimal point, revenue falls due to lower economic activity and higher evasion.

pages.title: Key Concepts
pages.intro: Tax Buoyancy and Tax Elasticity measure revenue responsiveness to GDP growth and policy changes respectively.

rows: Revenue growth from GDP growth + policy changes
Revenue growth from policy changes alone (GDP constant)
New tax law raises revenue 10% with no GDP growth

cards.front: What is the primary characteristic of Direct Taxes regarding incidence and impact?
cards.back: The incidence and impact fall on the same person.

cards.front: How are Direct Taxes classified in terms of their rate structure?
cards.back: They are progressive in nature, meaning higher income leads to higher tax.

cards.front: What is the primary characteristic of Indirect Taxes regarding incidence and impact?
cards.back: The impact and incidence fall on different persons.

cards.front: Why are Indirect Taxes considered regressive?
cards.back: They affect the poor more as a percentage of their income.

cards.back: It is a destination-based consumption tax.

cards.back: The relationship between tax rates and tax revenue.

cards.front: What is the definition of Tax Buoyancy?
cards.back: The responsiveness of tax growth to GDP growth.

parts.title: TNPSC Economy: GST & Fiscal Policy
parts.intro: Today we study the 'Taxes and Budgets'. Goods and Services Tax (GST) changed the indirect tax landscape of India. In TNPSC, 'GST Council' and 'Fiscal Deficit' are high-yield. Do you know which amendment introduced GST? Or what is the 'FRBM Act'? Let's master the revenue facts today.

pages.title: GST (One Nation One Tax)
pages.intro: Indirect tax implemented on 1 July 2017 via the 101st Constitutional Amendment, unifying multiple indirect taxes into a single nationwide tax.

items.label: Type
items.value: Indirect tax (collected by seller, paid to govt)

items.label: Replaced
items.value: Excise duty, sales tax, and other indirect taxes

pages.title: GST Council (Art 279A)
pages.intro: Constitutional body under Article 279A, chaired by the Union Finance Minister, that decides GST rates on goods and services.

blocks.text: The GST Council determines tax rates for the Goods and Services Tax. It was created by Article 279A of the Indian Constitution. The Chairman is the Union Finance Minister. Its primary role is to decide GST rates on different items.

pages.title: Fiscal Policy
pages.intro: Government decisions on revenue (taxes) and expenditure to control inflation and economic growth, managed by the Ministry of Finance.

pages.title: Fiscal Deficit
pages.intro: Total government borrowing in a year, calculated as total expenditure minus revenue receipts and non-debt capital receipts.

pages.title: FRBM Act (2003)
pages.intro: Law to reduce fiscal deficit, enforce financial discipline, and target fiscal deficit at 3% of GDP, with annual medium-term fiscal statements.

items.value: FRBM Act enacted to impose fiscal discipline

items.label: Original targets
items.value: Eliminate revenue deficit; fiscal deficit to 3% of GDP

items.label: Mandate
items.value: Present Medium-Term Fiscal Policy Statement annually

cards.front: When was the Goods and Services Tax (GST) implemented in India?
Which Constitutional Amendment introduced the GST?
What are the main GST rates since September 2025?
cards.back: 5% and 18%, with a 40% rate for luxury and sin goods (from 22 Sept 2025; earlier 5, 12, 18 and 28%).

cards.front: Which article of the Indian Constitution established the GST Council?
Who serves as the Chairman of the GST Council?
Which ministry is responsible for managing Fiscal Policy?
How is fiscal deficit calculated?
cards.back: Total Expenditure minus (Revenue Receipts + Non-debt Capital Receipts).

cards.front: What does the fiscal deficit measure?
cards.back: It measures the borrowing needs of the government.

cards.front: What was the original fiscal deficit target set by the FRBM Act (2003)?
cards.back: 3% of the country's Gross Domestic Product (GDP).
